title: Memory-Mapped I/O & Registers
relevance: Bare-metal and embedded SDE interviews test whether candidates can drive peripherals from C via MMIO, volatile access, and safe register bit manipulation without an OS.

phases.goal: Establish that peripherals are controlled by reading and writing fixed addresses in the same space as memory.

must_hit.point: Memory-Mapped I/O maps peripheral control and data registers into the same address space as program memory and RAM; reads/writes to those addresses trigger hardware actions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says MMIO puts peripheral registers in the CPU address map so ordinary loads/stores talk to hardware.

must_hit.point: A memory address in an embedded system may point to a physical wire or peripheral register, not only data storage.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts normal RAM addresses with addresses wired to GPIO/UART/timers via the data bus.

must_hit.point: MMIO reads and writes are not guaranteed symmetrical: a write may trigger an action and a read may return status or sensor data rather than the value written.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects the assumption that writing X then reading the same address returns X.

probes: What is memory-mapped I/O, and how does it differ from ordinary RAM?
If an address maps to a hardware timer that keeps ticking, what happens if you read that address twice in a row?

hints.1: Think about where a load or store actually goes on the chip’s bus.
hints.2: Some address ranges are RAM/Flash; others are wired to peripheral control circuits.
hints.3: MMIO means peripheral registers share the address space; accessing them causes hardware side effects, and read-back need not match what you wrote.

phases.goal: Show how C reaches hardcoded MMIO addresses safely and how bits in registers are updated.

must_hit.point: volatile on an MMIO pointer/member forbids the compiler from caching the value in a CPU register or optimizing away redundant reads and writes, because the hardware may change the location or a write may have side effects.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate ties volatile to hardware-owned state and side-effecting stores, not just ‘don’t optimize.’

must_hit.point: A raw MMIO access casts a hardcoded address to a pointer to volatile uint32_t and dereferences it; exact-width uint32_t matters because the silicon/bus may expect a 32-bit write.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes (volatile uint32_t *)addr style access and why char-width writes can be wrong.

must_hit.point: Read-modify-write bit updates use REG |= (1u << n) to set, REG &= ~(1u << n) to clear, and REG ^= (1u << n) to toggle.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes the three bitwise RMW idioms without inventing other operators.

must_hit.point: CMSIS-style access models a peripheral as a struct of volatile uint32_t registers at sequential offsets, mapped to a base address; silicon gaps need reserved padding fields so offsets stay aligned.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains GPIO_TypeDef-style layout, base cast, member access, and _reserved padding for missing registers.

probes: Why is volatile used when accessing hardware registers from C?
How would you set or clear a single bit in a peripheral register without disturbing other bits?
How does the CMSIS pattern map a block of registers to C?

hints.1: Ask what the compiler is allowed to assume about ordinary memory.
hints.2: Cover the cast-to-volatile-uint32_t idiom, then bit RMW, then struct-at-base-address.
hints.3: volatile forces real bus accesses; use |= / &= ~ / ^= for bits; model peripherals as structs of volatile uint32_t with padding for gaps.

phases.goal: Contrast unsafe C conveniences with portable, hardware-faithful register modeling.

must_hit.point: C bit-field layout within an integer is implementation-defined (packing direction can differ across compilers), so bit-fields are unsafe for hardware register layouts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites implementation-defined packing and risk when switching compilers or updating toolchains.

must_hit.point: For hardware registers, always use explicit bitwise masks and shifts rather than C bit-fields.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects bit-field structs for MMIO and insists on masks/shifts.

must_hit.point: Hundreds of individual register macros are tedious and error-prone compared with a CMSIS-style struct over sequential offsets at a base address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate prefers struct-mapped peripherals over one #define per register for maintainability and offset correctness.

probes: Would you model individual bits in a hardware register with C bit-fields? Why or why not?
Why prefer a peripheral struct over a pile of address macros?

hints.1: Think about what the C standard guarantees about bit packing.
hints.2: Compare bit-fields vs masks, and macros vs a struct at a base address.
hints.3: Bit-field order is implementation-defined—use masks/shifts; CMSIS structs keep offsets correct with less boilerplate.

phases.goal: Apply volatile MMIO access to real peripheral patterns and special register behaviors.

must_hit.point: A polling wait such as while a status flag bit is clear must use volatile so each iteration performs a fresh memory read; without it the compiler can optimize the loop into a hang.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate walks through a status-flag spin loop and names the missing-volatile infinite-loop failure.

must_hit.point: REG |= (1u << n) is not atomic: it becomes load, modify, store (three assembly instructions), so an interrupt that updates the same register between load and store can be overwritten on the delayed store.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains the RMW interrupt hazard on a shared register.

must_hit.point: Write-1-to-Clear (W1C) clears a flag by writing a 1 to that bit; writing 0 has no effect, which avoids RMW hazards on neighboring flags.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes writing 1 to clear and that zeros leave other bits alone.

must_hit.point: Special kinds include read-only status as const volatile uint32_t, write-only registers that return garbage or bus-fault on read, and side-effects on read such as reading a UART data register removing a byte from the receive queue.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists at least two of: const volatile RO, write-only, W1C, or read side effects.

probes: Why is volatile mandatory in a loop that waits for a hardware flag?
What goes wrong if an interrupt updates a register while your code does REG |= (1u << 5)?
How do write-1-to-clear flags differ from ordinary writable bits?

hints.1: Connect compiler optimization to a busy-wait on a status bit.
hints.2: Separate polling/volatile, RMW vs interrupts, then unusual register semantics.
hints.3: Without volatile, polling becomes if-then-infinite-loop; RMW is three instructions and interrupt-unsafe; W1C clears by writing 1.

tradeoffs.topic: C bit-fields vs explicit bitwise masks
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Bit-field layout is implementation-defined, so a compiler change can silently flip hardware configuration; for registers always use explicit masks and shifts.

Individual macros for every register are tedious and error-prone; a struct of volatile uint32_t members at a base address lets the compiler compute offsets, with reserved padding where silicon has gaps.

gotchas.trap: Assuming writing a value to an MMIO address means reading it back returns the same value
gotchas.correction: A write may trigger hardware action and a read may return status or sensor data; MMIO is not symmetrical storage.

gotchas.trap: Busy-waiting on a hardware flag without volatile
gotchas.correction: The compiler may turn while (*ptr == 0); into if (*ptr == 0) while (1); so the program never re-reads the hardware—especially under optimizations like -O2.

gotchas.trap: Treating REG |= (1u << n) as a single atomic update
gotchas.correction: It compiles to load, modify, and store; an interrupt between load and store can change the register and be overwritten by the late store.

gotchas.trap: Modeling register bits with C bit-fields
gotchas.correction: Packing order is implementation-defined; use explicit bitwise masks and shifts instead.

gotchas.trap: Clearing a W1C error flag by writing 0
gotchas.correction: Write a 1 to that bit to clear it; writing 0 has no effect and is the wrong mental model for W1C.
